intro: Every sport leaves paper behind. A newspaper notice announces a game. A club prints its rules. A league writes a charter that says who may join. A governor general buys a trophy and names trustees. Years later, a museum decides which objects to keep and which names to honor. Historians read all of these to learn what happened and who was left out.

This unit follows one sport, ice hockey, from painted Dutch canals and Mi'kmaq-carved sticks to the National Hockey League, the Colored Hockey League of Nova Scotia and the first women's Olympic tournament. Then it turns to objects and places: a stolen World Cup trophy, a gold medal made mostly of silver, a home plate marker in a Chicago parking lot, and the halls of fame and research groups that keep the record.

By the end, you can trace one sport through its documents and dates. You can tell a primary source from a later legend. You can explain how trophies, ballpark plans and archives shape memory. You can build an argument about a sport's past and name the record behind every claim.
bigQuestion: Who writes a sport's history, and how can we test their papers, objects and places against the record?

title: Capstone

chapters.title: One Sport and Its Paper: Ice Hockey
chapters.bigQuestion: What can the written record of one sport, from a newspaper notice to a league charter, show about who was let in and who was kept out?

story.title: A Notice in the Morning Paper
story.kicker: In March 1875 a Montreal newspaper told readers about a game on indoor ice, and a paper trail began.
paragraphs: On March 3, 1875, the Montreal Gazette told its readers about a game to be played that evening at the Victoria Skating Rink. The rink was an indoor building with a sheet of natural ice. A young engineer named James Creighton had gathered two teams of nine players each. Skaters in Montreal already knew stick games on frozen rivers and ponds.

The notice promised that spectators could watch in safety. The players would use a flat wooden disc instead of a ball, so it would not fly into the crowd. The next day the paper reported on the game. Historians still read that report closely, because it is one of the earliest printed accounts of an organized game of hockey indoors.

Over the next fifty years the paper stack grew. Montreal clubs printed a short set of rules in 1877. A governor general bought a silver bowl in 1892 and wrote conditions for winning it. Owners met in a Montreal hotel in 1917 and founded a new league. Each document added a rule, a trophy or a membership list.

Each paper also answered a quiet question: who may play here? For decades the answer on most rosters was white men and boys. Black players in Nova Scotia formed their own league, women organized their own teams, and the paper record shows when those doors opened.
story.think: Why might a historian trust a newspaper notice from 1875 more than a story told a hundred years later?

lessons.title: Stick Games on Frozen Water
lessons.mainIdea: People played stick-and-ball games on ice in Europe and North America long before anyone wrote down hockey's rules.
reading: Dutch painters of the early 1600s left some of the oldest pictures of games on ice. Hendrick Avercamp painted crowded winter scenes on frozen canals. In several of them, people swing curved sticks at a ball. The Dutch game was called *kolf*, and it was also played on land. The paintings show a pastime, not a league, with no fixed teams or lines.

In Britain and Ireland, people played field games with sticks and a ball under names such as bandy, shinty and hurling. When British soldiers and settlers came to Canada, they carried these games onto frozen rivers and lakes. On the ice, the games had no agreed size of team and no written rules. Each town and garrison played its own way.

The Mi'kmaq people of Nova Scotia played a stick-and-ball game of their own. In the 1800s, Mi'kmaq carvers made many of the hardwood hockey sticks sold in Canada, often from hornbeam trees. Their sticks were shipped to clubs across the country. This trade connects the sport's early equipment to Indigenous craft workers, whose names seldom appear in club records.

words.d: a Dutch stick-and-ball game of the 1600s, played on ice and on land
a stick-and-ball game on ice played in Britain and northern Europe
an Indigenous nation of Canada's Atlantic coast whose carvers made many early hockey sticks

lessons.title: Birthplace Claims and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Several towns claim to be the birthplace of hockey, but historians separate those legends from the earliest printed records.
reading: Windsor, Nova Scotia, says that boys at King's College School played hockey on a pond in the early 1800s. The town points to a passage in the writings of Thomas Chandler Haliburton, a Nova Scotia author who attended that school. Kingston, Ontario, and Montreal have made their own claims. Each town has a museum, a plaque or a local story to support it.

A *birthplace claim* is a statement that a sport began in one place. Such claims help towns attract visitors and take pride in a game. Historians ask a harder question: what written record, made at the time, shows the game being played? A memory written down decades later is weaker evidence than a newspaper printed the next morning.

By that test, the Montreal game of March 3, 1875, stands out. It was announced ahead of time and described afterward in print. That does not mean nobody played hockey earlier. It means 1875 is the earliest date that historians can tie to a public, organized indoor game with a *primary source* behind it.

words.d: a statement that a sport began in one particular town or place
a record made at the time of an event, such as a newspaper report printed the next day
a traditional story that is told as history but cannot be proven by records from the time

lessons.title: The Victoria Rink, 1875
lessons.mainIdea: An indoor rink in Montreal gave hockey a fixed room, a crowd and a newspaper audience in 1875.
reading: The Victoria Skating Rink opened in Montreal in 1862. It was a long brick building with a roof over natural ice. Members paid to skate there, and the rink held carnivals and costume balls. A roof meant the ice was protected from snow, and the walls marked the edges of the playing space.

On March 3, 1875, James Creighton brought two teams of nine players to the rink. Creighton had grown up in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and moved to Montreal as a young man. The players used a flat wooden *disc* instead of a ball. The Montreal Gazette said this choice would keep the object on the ice and protect the people watching.

The rink changed what hockey could become. A game in a building could be scheduled, advertised and watched by paying spectators. In 1883 Montreal's Winter Carnival held a hockey tournament, and in 1886 clubs formed the Amateur Hockey Association of Canada. A room, a crowd and a *club* came together, and written rules soon followed.

words.d: a building or space with a sheet of ice set aside for skating and games
the flat wooden object used in place of a ball at the 1875 game, an early form of the puck
a group of members who organize games and pay for a place to play

sections.title: Rules, a Trophy and a League

lessons.title: The Montreal Rules, 1877
lessons.mainIdea: In 1877 Montreal players printed a short set of hockey rules in the newspaper, borrowing from older field games.
reading: In February 1877 the Montreal Gazette printed seven rules for hockey. Students and club members in the city had drawn them up. Several rules were adapted from field hockey and rugby, which the players already knew. Printing the rules in a newspaper meant that anyone in Montreal could read the same text.

A written *code* lets strangers play together. Before 1877, a team from one town might argue with another about what was allowed. After the rules were printed, a captain could point to a sentence in the paper. McGill University students formed a hockey club in 1877, and they played under the new text.

The rules kept changing for decades. Team size fell from nine to seven by the 1880s, and later to six. Leagues added a *referee* to enforce the rules and a goal judge to rule on scores. Each change was voted on and printed, so historians can date many of them.

words.d: a written set of rules that players agree to follow
the official who enforces the rules during a game
the short set of hockey rules printed in the Montreal Gazette in 1877

lessons.title: Lord Stanley's Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: The Stanley Cup began in 1892 as a governor general's challenge trophy for amateur clubs and later became the prize of one professional league.
reading: Frederick Arthur Stanley, Lord Stanley of Preston, was Canada's governor general from 1888 to 1893. His children played hockey in Ottawa, and his daughter Isobel was photographed on the ice around 1890. In 1892 Lord Stanley bought a silver bowl in London. He gave it as a *challenge trophy* for Canada's best amateur hockey club.

Stanley named two *trustees* to hold the bowl and settle disputes. The champion club had to accept challenges from other clubs that qualified. The Montreal Hockey Club, part of the Montreal Amateur Athletic Association, was named the first holder in 1893. Stanley went home to England that year and never saw a Cup game.

Over time, professional teams took over. The Seattle Metropolitans of the Pacific Coast league became the first American team to win the Cup, in 1917. By 1926 only National Hockey League teams played for it. Winners' names are engraved on bands added to the base, so the object itself became a record.

words.d: a prize that the holder must defend against qualified challengers, rather than win in a fixed season
a person named to hold property and make decisions about it for a stated purpose
the British Crown's representative in Canada
the silver trophy Lord Stanley gave in 1892, later the championship prize of the National Hockey League

lessons.title: A New League in a Hotel
lessons.mainIdea: The National Hockey League was founded in a Montreal hotel in 1917, partly to shut one owner out of the old league.
reading: By the early 1900s, hockey players could be paid openly. The International Professional Hockey League, based in Michigan's Upper Peninsula and nearby towns, played from 1904 to 1907. In Canada the National Hockey Association began in 1909. Its owners quarreled often, especially with Eddie Livingstone, who owned a Toronto club.

On November 26, 1917, several owners met at the Windsor Hotel in Montreal. Instead of expelling Livingstone, they formed a new league without him: the National Hockey League. The first NHL season had four clubs, and one, the Montreal Wanderers, dropped out after its arena burned in January 1918. The league's founding shows that a *charter* can be written to exclude as well as to organize.

The NHL grew in the 1920s by selling *franchises*, the rights to own a team in a city. The Boston Bruins joined in 1924 as the first American club. In 1926 the Chicago Black Hawks, the Detroit club and the New York Rangers joined. The Black Hawks, owned by Frederic McLaughlin, won their first Stanley Cup in 1934.

words.d: a founding document that sets up an organization and says who belongs
the right, sold by a league, to own and run a team in a city
the professional league founded in Montreal on November 26, 1917
paid openly to play a sport

lessons.title: A Black League in Nova Scotia
lessons.mainIdea: Black players in Nova Scotia built their own hockey league in 1895, decades before the NHL had a Black player.
reading: Black communities in Nova Scotia date back to the late 1700s, when Black Loyalists arrived after the American Revolution. In Halifax and nearby towns, Black churches were centers of community life. In 1895, Black players and community leaders formed the Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes. Its teams came from towns around Halifax and Dartmouth.

The league played for decades, drawing crowds to games on outdoor and rink ice. White clubs and associations did not admit these teams, so the league created its own schedule and championships. Historians George and Darril Fosty told its story in their 2004 book *Black Ice*. Much of what is known comes from old newspapers and family memories gathered in that research.

The NHL's first Black player came much later. Willie O'Ree of Fredericton, New Brunswick, first played for the Boston Bruins in 1958. The gap between 1895 and 1958 shows that an unwritten *color line* can shape a sport even when no rule names race. The Colored Hockey League is one of the institutions that kept playing during those years.

lessons.title: Women on the Ice
lessons.mainIdea: Women played hockey from the 1890s, but world championships, Olympic events and college titles for women came only from 1990 on.
reading: Around 1890, Isobel Stanley, the governor general's daughter, was photographed playing hockey outdoors in Ottawa. By the 1890s, women's teams played at Canadian universities and in towns. They often played in long skirts. In the 1930s, the Preston Rivulettes of Ontario won many Canadian women's titles.

International bodies were slow to add women. The International Ice Hockey Federation held its first Women's World Championship in Ottawa in 1990, and Canada won. Women's hockey joined the Olympic program at Nagano, Japan, in 1998. The United States won that first Olympic gold medal, beating Canada in the final.

In American colleges, *Title IX* of 1972 pushed schools to add women's teams. The NCAA held its first national championship in women's ice hockey in 2001, won by the University of Minnesota Duluth. In 1992 goalie Manon Rhéaume played in an NHL preseason game for the Tampa Bay Lightning, the first woman to do so.

words.d: the 1972 federal law that bars sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money, including school sports
the world governing body of ice hockey, founded in Paris in 1908
the games played before a league's regular season begins

sections.title: A World Game with Written Rules

lessons.title: Paris, 1908, and the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: European nations founded an international hockey federation in 1908, and hockey entered the Olympic Games in 1920.
reading: On May 15, 1908, delegates met in Paris and founded the Ligue Internationale de Hockey sur Glace. Today it is called the International Ice Hockey Federation. Its first members were European, including France, Belgium, Switzerland, Great Britain and Bohemia. Canada and the United States joined in 1920.

Ice hockey first appeared at the Olympics in 1920 at Antwerp, Belgium, during the Summer Games. Canada sent the Winnipeg Falcons, a club made up mostly of players from Icelandic immigrant families. The Falcons won the gold medal. When the first Winter Olympics were held at Chamonix, France, in 1924, hockey moved there.

International hockey needed a shared rule book, because North American and European rinks and rules differed. The *federation* wrote rules for its tournaments. For decades the Olympics admitted only *amateurs*, so NHL players stayed home. NHL players first took part in the Olympic tournament in 1998.

words.d: a body that joins national associations and writes rules for international play
a player who is not paid to play; the Olympics long admitted only amateurs
the Canadian club that won the first Olympic hockey gold medal in 1920

look.text: In the early 1900s, a Canadian team used to its own rinks and rules traveled to play in Europe. The ice surface was a different size, and some rules on passing and substitutions were not the same. Officials from each side had learned different books.

lessons.title: Injuries and the Rule Book
lessons.mainIdea: A goalie's mask in 1959 and a player's death in 1968 pushed hockey toward rules requiring head protection.
reading: For decades most NHL goalies played without masks. On November 1, 1959, Montreal Canadiens goalie Jacques Plante was cut in the face by a shot during a game in New York. He returned wearing a mask he had made for practice. His coach had resisted, but Plante kept wearing it, and masks slowly became normal for goalies.

On January 13, 1968, Bill Masterton of the Minnesota North Stars hit his head on the ice during a game, and he died two days later. He was the first NHL player to die from an injury suffered in a game. The league later named a trophy for him. His death led many to call for *helmets*, but the league did not require them at once.

In 1979 the NHL adopted a rule that players entering the league after that year must wear helmets. Players already in the league could choose, under a *grandfather clause*. The last player to play without a helmet, Craig MacTavish, retired in 1997. The rule shows how leagues often change slowly, protecting new players while exempting veterans.

words.d: a hard hat worn to protect the head from injury
a rule that exempts people already in a group from a new requirement
an NHL award named for Bill Masterton, who died after a game injury in 1968

review.q: Why did NHL players stay out of the Olympics until 1998?
choices: The Olympics long admitted only amateurs
Hockey was not an Olympic sport

choices: Required helmets for every player at once
Required helmets for new players and let veterans choose

chapters.title: Objects, Plans and Archives
chapters.bigQuestion: How do trophies, ballpark plans, museums and archives shape what people believe about a sport's past?

story.title: A Letter from Denver
story.kicker: In 1907 a baseball commission trusted one old man's letter, and a legend got a museum.
paragraphs: In 1905, sporting-goods maker Albert Spalding set up a commission to decide where baseball came from. He had argued with the writer Henry Chadwick, who said the game grew from the English children's game of rounders. Spalding wanted an American origin. The commission was led by Abraham G. Mills, a former president of the National League.

The commission asked the public for memories. A mining engineer in Denver named Abner Graves wrote back. He said that in Cooperstown, New York, around 1839, a young man named Abner Doubleday had drawn a diagram of a new game. Graves was a boy at the time, and he wrote his letter more than sixty years later.

On December 30, 1907, the Mills Commission issued its report. It named Doubleday as baseball's inventor and Cooperstown as the place. Doubleday had died in 1893. He had become a Union general in the Civil War, and his own papers never mentioned baseball. In 1839 he was a cadet at West Point.

Historians have long rejected the story. Yet in 1939 the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum opened in Cooperstown, timed to a claimed hundredth birthday of the game. A single late letter helped decide where the sport's most famous museum stands.
story.think: Why do you think a commission in 1907 accepted a story from one letter written sixty years after the fact?

lessons.title: Older Papers About Baseball
lessons.mainIdea: Written records older than 1839 show that games called baseball existed before the Doubleday story says the game was invented.
reading: In 2004 a historian in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, drew attention to a town bylaw from 1791. It banned playing games such as "baseball" within eighty yards of the new meeting house, to protect its windows. The bylaw was written almost fifty years before 1839. It shows that a game with that name was already common enough to regulate.

The English novelist Jane Austen mentioned "base ball" in *Northanger Abbey*, written in the late 1790s and published in 1817. Her heroine enjoys the game as a girl. English children's books of the 1700s also printed rhymes about a game called base-ball. These sources point to a family of bat-and-base games brought to North America from England.

Historians call the Doubleday story an *origin myth*, a story that gives a sport a single inventor and a single birthday. The real history is a slow change, from folk games to club rules such as the Knickerbocker rules of 1845. The Pittsfield bylaw is a *municipal record*, a town document that recorded a problem, not a sport's triumph.

words.d: a story that gives something a single inventor, place and birthday, often without good evidence
a document kept by a town or city government, such as a bylaw or meeting minutes
a local rule made by a town or an organization
the group Albert Spalding set up in 1905 that named Abner Doubleday as baseball's inventor in 1907

look.title: Pittsfield Protects Its Windows, 1791
look.text: For the preservation of the windows in the new meeting house, no person shall play at wicket, cricket, baseball, batball, football, cricket or any other game of ball within eighty yards of the building.
look.cite: Town of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, bylaw of September 5, 1791
look.prompt: What problem was the town trying to solve, and why is this bylaw useful evidence for baseball's history?

check.q: What did the 1791 Pittsfield bylaw do?
choices: Banned ball games near the new meeting house
check.why: The bylaw protected the meeting house windows by banning ball games, including baseball, nearby.

check.q: Which novel by Jane Austen mentions base ball?
check.why: Austen's heroine in Northanger Abbey enjoys base ball as a girl.

check.q: Where was Abner Doubleday in 1839, according to the record?
check.why: Doubleday was a West Point cadet in 1839, which weakens the Cooperstown story.

lessons.title: A List of Olympic Victors
lessons.mainIdea: The famous date 776 BCE for the first Olympic Games comes from a list of winners compiled by Hippias of Elis around 400 BCE.
reading: Around 400 BCE, a scholar named Hippias of Elis compiled a list of Olympic victors. Elis was the city-state that ran the festival at Olympia. Hippias counted backward through the winners of the footrace called the *stadion*. His list began with a runner named Koroibos of Elis, dated to what we call 776 BCE.

Later Greek writers used this list to count time itself. They dated events by *Olympiads*, the four-year spans between festivals. The philosopher Aristotle also worked on a list of victors. Much later, Christian and Roman writers copied these lists, and the 776 BCE date passed into modern textbooks.

Modern historians treat the early part of the list with care. Hippias wrote more than three hundred years after the first names on it. He may have used local memories, temple records or guesses. Archaeology shows that people used the site at Olympia before 776 BCE, so the date marks the start of a list, not proof of the first games.

words.d: the short footrace at ancient Olympia, about one length of the stadium
the four-year span between Olympic festivals, used by Greeks to count years
the Greek scholar who compiled a list of Olympic victors around 400 BCE

look.title: A List Written Three Centuries Late
look.text: Imagine a writer in 2026 making a list of every winner of a village race back to the 1700s. For recent years, he has newspapers. For the oldest years, he has only a few family stories and a carved stone. He still writes one name for every year.
look.prompt: Which parts of his list would you trust most, and how is his task like Hippias's?

check.q: Who compiled the list of Olympic victors that begins in 776 BCE?
check.why: Hippias of Elis compiled the list around 400 BCE.

check.q: What is an Olympiad?
choices: The four-year span between Olympic festivals
check.why: Greeks counted years in Olympiads, the four-year spans between festivals.

check.q: Why do historians treat the early part of the list with care?
choices: It was compiled more than three hundred years after the first names
check.why: Hippias wrote long after the first races and may have relied on memory or guesses.

lessons.title: William Webb Ellis and a Plaque
lessons.mainIdea: The story that William Webb Ellis invented rugby in 1823 rests on a letter written more than fifty years later, yet the World Cup trophy bears his name.
reading: A plaque at Rugby School in England says that in 1823 a pupil named William Webb Ellis picked up the ball and ran with it, in disregard of the football rules of his time. The story first appeared in 1876, in a letter by Matthew Bloxam, a former pupil. Bloxam had left the school before 1823 and did not see the event himself.

In 1895 the Old Rugbeian Society, a club of former pupils, looked into the story. It found no one who could confirm it. Webb Ellis had died in 1872, in France, after a career as a clergyman. He never claimed to have started a new game. Still, the society accepted the tale, and the school honored him.

The story shows how an institution can adopt a legend. When the first *Rugby World Cup* was held in 1987, its trophy was called the Webb Ellis Cup. Historians describe rugby's real history as a slow split among school football codes, leading to the Rugby Football Union in 1871. The *plaque* is a record of what people later believed.

words.d: a flat sign of metal or stone placed on a wall to honor a person or event
the international rugby union championship first held in 1987
the governing body for rugby in England, founded in 1871
a club of former Rugby School pupils that looked into the Webb Ellis story in 1895

look.title: What a Plaque Records
look.text: A stone plaque says that a boy picked up a ball and ran with it in 1823. A letter from 1876 is the earliest known written version of the story. The man who wrote it was not there. The boy himself never mentioned it before he died in 1872.
look.prompt: What does the plaque prove, and about whom? Explain the difference between proof of an event and proof of a belief.

check.q: When did the Webb Ellis story first appear in writing?
check.why: Matthew Bloxam's 1876 letter is the earliest known written version.

check.q: What did the Old Rugbeian Society find in 1895?
choices: No one who could confirm the story
check.why: The society found no witness who could confirm it, yet accepted the tale.

check.q: What is the Webb Ellis Cup?
choices: The trophy of the Football Association
The trophy of the Rugby World Cup, first held in 1987
check.why: The Rugby World Cup's trophy, first awarded in 1987, carries Webb Ellis's name.

lessons.title: A Trophy Stolen Twice
lessons.mainIdea: The first soccer World Cup trophy was stolen in 1966 and found by a dog, then stolen again in 1983 and never recovered.
reading: The first FIFA World Cup trophy was a gilded statue of a winged figure. It was later named for Jules Rimet, the FIFA president who pushed for the tournament. In March 1966, months before England hosted the World Cup, the trophy was stolen from a public exhibition in London. A week later, a dog named Pickles found it wrapped in newspaper under a hedge in south London.

FIFA's rules said that a nation winning the trophy three times would keep it for good. Brazil won its third title in 1970 in Mexico and took the Jules Rimet Trophy home permanently. It was displayed at the offices of the Brazilian football confederation in Rio de Janeiro. In December 1983 thieves stole it there, and it has never been found.

FIFA commissioned a new trophy, designed by the Italian artist Silvio Gazzaniga, first awarded in 1974. Under newer rules, winners do not keep the original; they receive a *replica*. The two thefts show that a trophy is more than a prize. It is an *artifact*, an object that carries a nation's memory, and losing it cannot be undone.

words.d: an object made by people that historians study for what it shows about the past
an exact copy of an object, made to stand in for the original
the first FIFA World Cup trophy, kept by Brazil in 1970 and stolen in 1983

look.title: A Rule About Keeping
look.text: Rule A, used until 1970: a nation that wins the trophy three times keeps it for good. Rule B, used from 1974: winners hold the original only briefly and take home a copy, while the original stays with the governing body.
look.prompt: What problem might FIFA have been trying to avoid with Rule B, and what did Rule A reward?

check.q: Who found the stolen World Cup trophy in London in 1966?
check.why: A dog named Pickles found it under a hedge in south London about a week after the theft.

check.q: Why did Brazil keep the Jules Rimet Trophy after 1970?
choices: It had won the World Cup three times
check.why: FIFA's rule gave the trophy for good to the first nation to win three times; Brazil did in 1970.

check.q: What happened to the Jules Rimet Trophy in 1983?
choices: It was stolen in Rio de Janeiro and never recovered
check.why: Thieves stole it from the Brazilian confederation's offices in December 1983.

lessons.title: What a Gold Medal Is Made Of
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic medals changed from silver for winners in 1896 to solid gold by 1904 and to gold-plated silver after 1912.
reading: At the first modern Olympics in Athens in 1896, winners received a silver medal and an olive branch. Runners-up received a bronze or copper medal. Third place received nothing official. The now-familiar order of gold, silver and bronze was first used at the 1904 Games in St. Louis.

The 1912 Games in Stockholm were the last to award medals of *solid gold*. After that, the cost of gold made such medals too expensive. Modern rules from the International Olympic Committee say a gold medal must be mostly silver and *plated* with at least six grams of pure gold. Each host city designs its own medal within those rules.

A medal's metal tells a story about money and meaning. The word gold stays in the name even though the object is mostly silver. Collectors and museums prize medals from 1912 and earlier. Some athletes have sold their medals, and some Olympic medals have been reissued after officials changed results.

words.d: made entirely of gold, not a coating over another metal
covered with a thin layer of another metal
the body that governs the Olympic Games and sets rules for them

look.title: Two Medals in a Case
look.text: A museum case holds two first-place Olympic medals. One, from Athens in 1896, is silver and came with an olive branch. The other, from a Games in the 2000s, is called a gold medal, but most of its metal is silver under a gold coating.
look.prompt: What do the two medals show about how the meaning and cost of a prize changed over time?

check.q: What did winners receive at the 1896 Athens Olympics?
choices: A silver medal and an olive branch
check.why: In 1896 winners got silver medals and olive branches; runners-up got bronze or copper.

check.q: Which Games were the last to award solid gold medals?
check.why: Stockholm in 1912 was the last Games with solid gold medals.

check.q: What does plated mean?
choices: Covered with a thin layer of another metal
check.why: Modern gold medals are silver plated with at least six grams of gold.

lessons.title: Two Typed Pages at Auction
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith's original typed rules for basketball sold at auction in 2010 and now sit on display at the University of Kansas.
reading: James Naismith's original rules for basketball fit on two typed pages from December 1891. The pages stayed with his family for decades. In December 2010 the auction house Sotheby's sold them in New York. David Booth, an investor who had studied at the University of Kansas, paid about 4.3 million dollars.

Booth gave the pages to the University of Kansas, where Naismith had coached and taught from 1898. The university built a new home for them, the DeBruce Center, which opened in 2016 next to Allen Fieldhouse. The pages are shown behind glass with controlled light. An *auction* moved a family keepsake into public view.

The sale raised questions that historians and collectors still discuss. Should key sports documents belong to families, private buyers or public museums? A *provenance*, the record of who owned an object and when, helps buyers trust that a document is real. The Naismith pages had a clear line of ownership from the inventor to his family.

words.d: a public sale where buyers bid against each other and the highest bid wins
the record of who owned an object and when, used to show it is genuine
an auction house that sold Naismith's original basketball rules in 2010

look.title: Three Possible Owners
look.text: A family owns an important sports document. Option one: keep it at home. Option two: sell it at auction to the highest bidder. Option three: give it to a public museum. In 2010 the Naismith family chose an auction, and the buyer then gave the pages to a university.
look.prompt: Which option best protects a document for historians, and which best rewards the family? Explain the tradeoff.

check.q: Who bought Naismith's original rules at auction in 2010?
check.why: David Booth, a Kansas alumnus, bought the pages for about 4.3 million dollars.

check.q: Where are the original rules displayed today?
choices: The DeBruce Center at the University of Kansas
check.why: Booth gave them to Kansas, which opened the DeBruce Center in 2016.

check.q: What is provenance?
choices: The place a sport was invented
The record of who owned an object and when
check.why: Provenance traces ownership and helps show an object is genuine.

lessons.title: A Home Plate in a Parking Lot
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's first Comiskey Park stood from 1910 to 1991, and a marker in a parking lot now shows where its home plate was.
reading: Comiskey Park opened on Chicago's South Side on July 1, 1910. White Sox owner Charles Comiskey built it of steel and concrete. The architect was Zachary Taylor Davis, who later designed the park now called Wrigley Field. Concrete stands replaced wooden ones, which often burned.

The park hosted the first Major League All-Star Game in 1933. It also hosted the East-West All-Star Game of the Negro Leagues from 1933 on. The White Sox played their last game there on September 30, 1990. A new park opened across 35th Street in 1991, and the old one was torn down that year.

Today the site of the old park is a parking lot. A marble *marker* painted into the pavement shows where home plate stood. The architect's *site plan*, the drawing of where the park sat on its block, helps historians match old photographs to the ground. A marker turns an empty lot into a record of a building.

words.d: a measured drawing showing where a building sits on its piece of land
a sign or plate placed on the ground or a wall to show where something happened
a person who designs buildings and draws their plans

look.title: Standing on the Old Plate
look.text: A visitor stands on a marble plate set into a parking lot on Chicago's South Side. Cars fill the spaces around it. Across the street rises a newer ballpark. Old photographs show that, from this spot, a batter once faced a double-decked grandstand.
look.prompt: What would a historian need, besides the marker, to picture the old park accurately?

check.q: When did the first Comiskey Park open?
check.why: Comiskey Park opened on July 1, 1910.

check.q: Which game was first held at Comiskey Park in 1933?
choices: The first Major League All-Star Game
check.why: Comiskey Park hosted the first Major League All-Star Game in 1933.

check.q: What does a site plan show?
choices: Where a building sits on its land
check.why: A site plan is a measured drawing of a building's place on its land.

lessons.title: Lights at Wrigley, 1988
lessons.mainIdea: Wrigley Field played only day games until 1988, when the city allowed a limited number of night games.
reading: Other major league parks added lights for night games starting in 1935, in Cincinnati. The Cubs' owner, Philip K. Wrigley, planned to add lights in 1941. After the attack on Pearl Harbor that December, he gave the steel and wiring to the war effort. For decades afterward, the Cubs played every home game in daylight.

Wrigley Field sits in a crowded neighborhood of homes and apartments. Neighbors worried that night games would bring noise, traffic and late crowds. In the 1980s, state and city rules restricted night games there. In 1988 the Chicago City Council approved lights, with a limit on how many night games the Cubs could play each season.

The first night game at Wrigley began on August 8, 1988, but rain stopped it before it became official. The first completed night game came the next evening, August 9. The fight over lights shows that a ballpark is part of a city's *zoning*, the rules about how land in each area may be used. A *city council* can shape a team's schedule.

words.d: city rules about how land in each area may be used
the elected body that makes local laws for a city
a law passed by a city or town government

look.title: Two Sides of Clark Street
look.text: A team owner says night games would let working fans attend and would bring more television money. A neighbor across the street says she wants to sleep, park her car and walk home safely. The city council must write one rule for both.
look.prompt: What kind of rule might balance both sides, and how does the 1988 limit on night games fit?

check.q: Why did Philip K. Wrigley not add lights in 1941?
choices: The league did not allow night games
He gave the materials to the war effort after Pearl Harbor
check.why: After Pearl Harbor, he donated the steel and wiring to the war effort.

check.q: When was the first completed night game at Wrigley Field?
check.why: The August 8 game was rained out, so the first completed night game was August 9, 1988.

check.q: What is zoning?
choices: City rules about how land in each area may be used
check.why: Zoning rules decide how land may be used, which shaped the fight over lights.

lessons.title: Camden Yards Looks Backward
lessons.mainIdea: Oriole Park at Camden Yards, opened in 1992, used an old warehouse and an old-style plan, and many cities copied it.
reading: From the 1960s to the 1980s, many cities built round, concrete stadiums for both baseball and football. The Orioles' new park in Baltimore went the other way. Oriole Park at Camden Yards opened on April 6, 1992. It was built for baseball only, on the site of an old railroad yard downtown.

The design kept the long brick warehouse of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad beyond right field. The park used steel and brick to look like ballparks of the early 1900s. The Maryland Stadium Authority, a state body, paid for and owned it. The architecture firm HOK Sport led the design.

Camden Yards began a wave of *retro ballparks*, new parks built to look old. Cleveland, Denver, San Francisco and Pittsburgh soon opened parks in the same style. The plan shows that design copies design. It also shows *adaptive reuse*, keeping an old building and giving it a new job.

words.d: a new ballpark designed to look like the parks of the early 1900s
keeping an old building and giving it a new purpose
the state body that paid for and owns Oriole Park at Camden Yards

look.title: Ballparks Built After Camden Yards
look.cite: Major League Baseball ballpark records; opening dates as published by each club
look.prompt: How many years passed between Camden Yards and PNC Park, and what does the list suggest about how design ideas spread?

check.q: When did Oriole Park at Camden Yards open?
check.why: The park opened on April 6, 1992.

check.q: What old building did Camden Yards keep beyond right field?
choices: A Baltimore and Ohio Railroad warehouse
check.why: The design kept the long B&O warehouse as part of the park.

check.q: What is a retro ballpark?
choices: A new park designed to look like early-1900s parks
A park that hosts only old-timers' games
A round stadium for two sports
check.why: Camden Yards began a wave of new parks built in an old style.

lessons.title: Halls of Fame Choose Places
lessons.mainIdea: Each sport's hall of fame chose a town tied to a story about its beginning, from Cooperstown to Canton.
reading: The National Baseball Hall of Fame held its first election in 1936. Voters chose five players: Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth, Honus Wagner, Christy Mathewson and Walter Johnson. The museum opened in Cooperstown, New York, on June 12, 1939. Its location rested on the Doubleday legend.

Other sports followed. The Hockey Hall of Fame was established in 1943 and later built a home in Toronto. The Pro Football Hall of Fame opened in 1963 in Canton, Ohio, because the league that became the NFL was founded there in 1920, in a car showroom. The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame opened in 1959 at Springfield, Massachusetts.

A hall of fame is a *museum* and a voting body at once. Its members, called *inductees*, are chosen by committees or writers. Those choices decide whose names and objects are preserved. For decades, Negro Leagues stars and women athletes were missing from many halls, until special committees began adding them.

words.d: a museum that honors chosen people in a field and keeps their objects and records
a person voted into a hall of fame
a building that collects, keeps and shows objects for the public

look.title: When Sports Halls of Fame Began
look.cite: Official histories of each hall of fame
look.prompt: The women's basketball hall came decades after the others. What does that gap suggest about whose history was collected first?

check.q: Which five players were chosen in the first Baseball Hall of Fame election in 1936?
choices: Robinson, Doby, Paige, Gibson and Bell
Cobb, Ruth, Wagner, Mathewson and Johnson
Gehrig, DiMaggio, Williams, Musial and Mays
Cobb, Ruth, Gehrig, Young and Foxx
check.why: Voters chose Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth, Honus Wagner, Christy Mathewson and Walter Johnson.

check.q: Why is the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio?
choices: The first Super Bowl was played there
The league that became the NFL was founded there in 1920
check.why: The league was founded in a Canton car showroom in 1920.

choices: A person voted into a hall of fame

lessons.title: Researchers Build the Record
lessons.mainIdea: Groups of researchers, such as SABR and Retrosheet, and libraries such as the LA84 Foundation's, gather and check the records sports history depends on.
reading: In August 1971 a small group of baseball researchers met in Cooperstown. Led by L. Robert Davids, they founded the Society for American Baseball Research, known as *SABR*. Members, many of them unpaid, dig through old newspapers and box scores. They correct records, write biographies and publish research journals.

In 1989 David Smith founded Retrosheet, a project to collect the *play-by-play* of old major league games. Volunteers type up scorebooks and newspaper accounts so that the record of each game can be checked. Their work has helped fix errors in official statistics. The data is free for anyone to use.

Some archives came from the Games themselves. The 1984 Los Angeles Olympics ended with a surplus, and part of it created a foundation in Southern California, now called the LA84 Foundation. Its library holds books, magazines and Olympic reports open to researchers. An *archive* like this keeps paper that clubs and leagues might throw away.

words.d: the Society for American Baseball Research, founded in Cooperstown in 1971
a record of every play in a game, in order
a collection of old documents and records kept for study
money left over after all costs are paid

look.title: Two Box Scores, One Game
look.text: A researcher finds two newspaper box scores for the same 1910 game. One credits a batter with two hits, the other with three. The official record has used the first paper for a century. The researcher checks a third paper and the team's own scorebook, and both show three hits.
look.prompt: Should the official record change? What evidence would you want before deciding?

check.q: Where was SABR founded in 1971?

check.q: What does Retrosheet collect?
choices: The play-by-play of old major league games

check.q: Where did the LA84 Foundation's money come from?
choices: Part of the surplus from the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics

choices: That Alexander Cartwright wrote the first rules
That Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown
review.why: The commission named Doubleday and Cooperstown, based largely on Abner Graves's letter.

choices: The Hall of Fame opening of 1939

review.q: What do the Doubleday and Webb Ellis stories have in common?
choices: Both are proven by eyewitness diaries

review.q: What happened to the Jules Rimet Trophy?
choices: Stolen in 1966 and found, then stolen in 1983 and never recovered
review.why: Pickles found it in 1966; it was stolen again in Rio in 1983.

review.q: Which statement about Olympic gold medals is correct?
choices: They have always been solid gold

review.q: What does the Wrigley Field lights story show?
choices: City rules and neighbors can shape a team's schedule
Lights were banned in all ballparks

choices: It shows who owned an object and helps prove it is real
It names the inventor of a sport
